content: The updated guidelines for managing HIV care include several key recommendations and changes to improve patient outcomes and streamline monitoring systems. These updates address various aspects of HIV care, including treatment initiation, monitoring, and integration with other health services. Below is a detailed explanation of the updates: 1. Management of Infants and Children Failing First-Line Regimens: New approaches to infant prophylaxis have been introduced, including defining high-risk infants and determining the appropriate duration and number of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). 2. Routine Monitoring and Treatment Failure Diagnosis: CD4 counts are now recommended only at baseline to identify patients with severe or advanced HIV infection who require fast-tracking and screening for opportunistic infections. Routine viral load monitoring is emphasized at 6, 12, and 24 months to confirm treatment success or failure, where available. 3. Coinfections and Comorbidities: Updated guidance includes the use of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, improved diagnosis and management of tuberculosis (TB) using tools like Xpert MTB/RIF and lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assays, and presumptive TB treatment for critically ill patients. Additionally, there is a focus on managing non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular diseases and depression, as well as other co-conditions like viral hepatitis (HBV and HCV), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and opioid substitution therapy for people who inject drugs. 4. Differentiated Care Models: Recommendations include decentralizing ART initiation and maintenance to peripheral health facilities, community-based ARV distribution by trained lay providers, and reducing clinic visits and medication pickups for stable patients. Patient tracking and service delivery are tailored to individual needs. 5. HIV Patient Monitoring Tools: The use of standardized HIV patient cards and ART registers is recommended at all ART-providing sites, including antenatal care (ANC) and TB clinics. These tools facilitate continuity of care as patients move between facilities. 6. Transition from Pre-ART Registers: The pre-ART register, previously used to monitor patients not yet eligible for ART, is no longer required since all confirmed HIV-positive individuals are now eligible for treatment under the treat all approach. 7. Strategic Information and Indicators: Simplified and prioritized indicators are organized within a cascade framework to optimize data collection and reporting. These indicators align with WHO's 2015 consolidated guidelines on strategic information for HIV in the health sector. 8. Integration of Services: HIV care is integrated with other services such as family planning, STI management, and TB treatment in high-burden settings. 9. Minimum Dataset for Patient Monitoring: A core set of demographic, clinical, and laboratory data elements has been standardized to provide a comprehensive assessment of all people living with HIV. This dataset supports clinical care and program monitoring while enabling data comparison across populations and settings. 10. Universal ART Initiation: Updates reflect the transition to universal ART initiation, removing previous eligibility criteria. New data elements include prior ARV use (e.g., PrEP and PEP), district of residence, family status, and date of first HIV-positive test. 11. ART Regimen Updates: Changes include newly recommended ARV regimens, third-line regimen switches, and updates on reasons for non-adherence, drug substitutions, and stopping ART. Clinical staging is no longer required for routine monitoring but may be used at enrollment to identify advanced disease in the absence of CD4 counts. 12. Retention and Outcomes: Retention in HIV care is defined as patients who are alive and receiving routine care, including ART, at specific time points. Efforts to contact patients who miss appointments are emphasized to improve retention and outcomes. 13. Transfer and Tracking of Patients: Patients transferring in are categorized based on their ART status and previous records. 14. Key Populations and Vulnerable Groups: Special attention is given to key populations at higher risk of HIV, such as men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Vulnerable groups, including adolescents, orphans, and migrant workers, are also addressed. 15. TB and HIV Integration: Active TB disease and latent TB infection (LTBI) are defined, with guidance on diagnosis and treatment. TB preventive therapy is emphasized to reduce the risk of reactivation. 16. Community Health Worker Involvement: Community health workers engaged in ART delivery are encouraged to monitor and report on key activities in a standardized manner. 17. Transition to Electronic Systems: The guidance supports transitioning from paper-based to electronic systems for improved monitoring and reporting. 18. Focus on Patient-Centered Care: The updated guidelines aim to support patient monitoring as individuals move between health facilities over time, ensuring continuity and quality of care. These updates reflect the latest evidence and WHO recommendations, aiming to enhance the quality of HIV care, improve patient outcomes, and streamline program monitoring and evaluation.
